summary: EcoFilter Intelligence is a research-based engineering concept that explores a modular approach to reducing selected industrial air pollutants while allowing production to continue. The project connects environmental data with a proposed multi-stage filtration tower. The concept includes a pre-filter for particles, catalytic oxidation research for carbon monoxide, an adsorption stage proposed for nitrogen dioxide, limestone-based flue-gas desulfurization for sulfur dioxide, and electrostatic precipitation for particulate matter. A final monitoring chamber uses sensors and an ESP32-based dashboard concept to display parameters such as airflow, pressure, and pollutant readings, helping indicate system conditions and maintenance needs. NASA resources, such as satellite air-quality observations and atmospheric data, support the trend investigation. The website presents the engineering design, research evidence, and simulated dashboard values. EcoFilter has not been built or experimentally validated; therefore, no removal efficiency or measured performance is claimed. It is a proposed concept for study and testing under real industrial conditions.
details:
EcoFilter Intelligence – Project Description EcoFilter Intelligence is a research-based engineering concept designed to explore smarter ways of reducing industrial air pollution without requiring permanent interruption of industrial production. The project proposes a modular, multi-stage filtration tower that targets different pollutants through specialized treatment stages. It includes a pre-filter for large particles, a catalytic oxidation stage proposed for carbon monoxide (CO), an adsorption stage investigated for nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), limestone-based flue-gas desulfurization for sulfur dioxide (SO₂), and an electrostatic precipitator for particulate matter such as PM2.5 and PM10. The system also proposes an intelligent monitoring chamber using an ESP32-based architecture and environmental sensors to monitor parameters such as airflow, pressure, and pollutant concentrations. A digital dashboard concept presents this information and helps identify possible maintenance needs. The project combines NASA Earth observation resources, including OMI and MODIS data, with engineering research to investigate air pollution trends and connect environmental evidence with a potential engineering solution. Its main benefit is presenting a modular and potentially adaptable approach to industrial emission control, supporting environmental awareness, cleaner industrial processes, and more informed maintenance decisions. The creative aspect is the integration of satellite-based environmental research, multi-stage filtration technologies, and smart monitoring within one proposed engineering concept. The website was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with interactive visualizations and simulated dashboard data. Research also involved NASA datasets, scientific publications, and engineering references. Important development factors included pollutant-specific treatment methods, industrial continuity, modular design, monitoring requirements, maintenance, and scientific reliability. EcoFilter Intelligence is currently a proposed concept. It has not been physically built or experimentally validated, and its removal efficiency and operational performance remain to be tested.

Research-Based Filtration Performance The proposed EcoFilter system is based on established air pollution control technologies. Published research reports removal efficiencies of 90–100% for carbon monoxide in specific catalytic oxidation tube tests. Industrial wet flue-gas desulfurization systems can achieve up to 99% SO₂ removal, while electrostatic precipitators can achieve approximately 99.5% particulate matter removal in certain industrial applications. These figures represent reported performance of individual technologies under specific operating conditions, not the performance of EcoFilter Intelligence. The nitrogen dioxide adsorption stage remains under research, and its efficiency requires further experimental validation. The overall system efficiency has not yet been determined and will depend on gas composition, temperature, airflow, contact time, filter materials, and system design.
